title: Authentication Methods
subtitle: How one user proves who they are, from passwords to passkeys.
throughline: One user proving their identity, followed from a typed password through one-time codes and passkeys to a layered, multi-factor sign-in.

chapters.title: Knowledge Factors
chapters.blurb: The user proves identity with a password, and the server stores only a salted, slow hash of it.

story.title: Knowledge Factors
story.subtitle: How one user proves who they are, from passwords to passkeys.

steps.title: Knowledge Factors
steps.narration: **Password authentication** is the simplest method: the user proves identity with *something they know*. The server's job is to store that secret safely.
steps.say: We begin with the oldest idea in authentication: proving who you are with something only you know.
steps.coverSubtitle: Something the user knows: a password the server never stores in the clear.

steps.title: The user submits a password
steps.narration: The user defines a **password** at registration and *proves identity by entering it*. The **app server** receives the submitted secret on sign-in.
steps.say: Our user sets a password when registering, then later proves identity by entering it. The app server receives that typed secret.

steps.title: Never store it in the clear
steps.narration: User passwords **must be hashed before storage**. Hashing is a *one-way transformation* that can't be reversed, so the raw password is never exposed if the database is breached.
steps.say: The server must never keep that password as-is. Passwords are hashed before storage, a one-way transformation that cannot be reversed.

steps.title: A slow hash on purpose
steps.narration: Use a **strong password hash** like `Argon2` or `bcrypt`. These deliberately *use significant compute*, which drastically slows brute-force attacks against weak passwords.
steps.say: Because user passwords are often weak, the server uses a strong hash algorithm designed for passwords. It burns significant compute, which drastically slows brute-force attacks.

steps.title: Salt every hash
steps.narration: The hash **must be salted**: a random *nonce unique to each hash*, combined with the password during hashing. Generate **at least 16 random bytes**.
steps.say: Each hash must be salted. A salt is a random nonce, unique to each hash, combined with the password. At least sixteen random bytes is the recommendation.

steps.title: Salt defeats rainbow tables
steps.narration: Salting ensures *identical passwords produce unique hashes*, preventing attackers from pre-computing hashes for common passwords — so-called **rainbow tables**.
steps.say: Salting ensures that even identical passwords produce unique hashes. That stops attackers from pre-computing hashes for common passwords, the trick known as rainbow tables.

steps.title: Verify in constant time
steps.narration: Verification *hashes the provided input* and compares it with the **stored hash**. The comparison runs as a **constant-time operation** to mitigate timing attacks.
steps.say: To verify, the server hashes the provided input the same way and compares it with the stored hash. That comparison runs in constant time to mitigate timing attacks.

steps.title: But knowledge alone is fragile
steps.narration: Even so, *passwords come with risks*: weak or reused passwords, forgotten ones, and **phishing**. A breached hash database can put *other websites* at risk too, motivating a second factor.
steps.say: Even hashed and salted, knowledge factors stay fragile. Users pick weak passwords, reuse them, forget them, or get phished. That is why one factor is rarely enough.

chapters.title: Possession Factors
chapters.blurb: A second factor the user has: one-time codes by email or SMS, and codes from an authenticator app.

story.title: Possession Factors
story.subtitle: How one user proves who they are, from passwords to passkeys.

steps.title: Possession Factors
steps.narration: Because passwords are often *not strong enough*, sites add a secondary method — **two-factor** or **multi-factor authentication**. The new factor is *something the user has*.
steps.say: Because passwords alone are often not strong enough, our user now adds a second factor: something they have.
steps.coverSubtitle: Something the user has: a one-time code that proves control of a channel or device.

steps.title: Password is still step one
steps.narration: The user still **submits the password** to the app server first. A valid password is now only *the first of two checks* before access is granted.
steps.say: Our user starts the same way, sending the password to the app server. But now a successful password is only the first of two checks.

steps.title: The server mints a one-time code
steps.narration: The server generates a **one-time code** with *at least 40 bits of entropy* — an 8-character alphanumeric code — valid for *at most one hour*.
steps.say: The app server generates a fresh one-time code. The page recommends at least forty bits of entropy, an eight-character alphanumeric code, valid for at most one hour.

steps.title: Sent to the email address
steps.narration: The code is sent to the user's **email address**. Entering it proves *control of that inbox*. The code itself is bound to the session that started the attempt.
steps.say: One delivery channel is the user's email address. The code is sent there, and entering it proves the user controls that inbox.

steps.title: Or to a phone over SMS
steps.narration: A common secondary method is a **one-time code sent over SMS** to the user's phone number, proving possession of *that phone*.
steps.say: Another common channel is a phone number over text message. A one-time code sent by S M S proves possession of that phone.

steps.title: Or generated by an app
steps.narration: Codes can instead be *generated by an* **authenticator app** on a mobile device, with nothing sent over a network for an attacker to intercept.
steps.say: A third option needs no delivery at all. An authenticator app on a mobile device generates codes locally that the server can verify.

steps.title: The user enters the code
steps.narration: The user enters the code and the server **verifies** it. The code is *hashed with Argon2 or bcrypt* and gated by a rate limit of about **1 attempt per minute** using a token bucket.
steps.say: However it arrived, the user reads the code and enters it. The server hashes and verifies it under a strict rate limit of one attempt per minute.

steps.title: Weak alone, useful together
steps.narration: These methods are *relatively weak on their own*. Combined with passwords they give *reasonable security*, mainly by **slowing an attack** long enough for the real user to reset credentials.
steps.say: These secondary methods are relatively weak on their own. Their real value is to slow an attack down long enough for the legitimate user to reset their credentials.

chapters.title: Passwordless and Passkeys
chapters.blurb: Ditching the password: one-time email codes or links, and WebAuthn passkeys built on public-key cryptography.

story.title: Passwordless and Passkeys
story.subtitle: How one user proves who they are, from passwords to passkeys.

steps.title: Passwordless and Passkeys
steps.narration: Another option is to *ditch passwords altogether*: passwordless sign-in with **one-time codes or links**, and ultimately **passkeys**.
steps.say: Now our user ditches the password altogether, first with one-time codes, then with passkeys.
steps.coverSubtitle: Ditch the password: one-time codes and links, then passkeys built on public-key cryptography.

steps.title: Sign in with no password
steps.narration: The user requests sign-in with **no password**. The app server runs a *passwordless flow*, similar to an email-based password reset flow.
steps.say: The user wants to sign in but has no password to give. The app server runs a passwordless flow, much like an email-based reset flow.

steps.title: A one-time code or link
steps.narration: The server issues a **one-time code or link** and delivers it to the user. Because *the server controls the complexity*, it can be **more secure than a password**.
steps.say: The server issues a one-time code or link and delivers it to the user. Because the server controls its complexity, these can be more secure than a user-chosen password.

steps.title: Only as secure as the inbox
steps.narration: The main risk: the code or link is **only as secure as the user's email account and device**. These methods can be *enough for most websites* but not as strong as a password with two-factor.
steps.say: There is a catch. The code or link is only as secure as the user's email account and device. Lose the inbox, and you lose the account.

steps.title: Enter the passkey
steps.narration: **Passkeys** are secure credentials that use *public-key cryptography*, based on the **Web Authentication API**, or WebAuthn. The private key stays in an **authenticator**.
steps.say: For the highest security, our user reaches for a passkey. It is a secure credential stored on the device or in a password manager, built on the Web Authentication API.

steps.title: The server sends a challenge
steps.narration: The server generates a **challenge**; the **browser** calls `navigator.credentials.get()` with `userVerification: "required"`, prompting a *PIN or biometrics*.
steps.say: Authentication starts with the server generating a challenge. The browser receives it and calls navigator dot credentials dot get, with user verification set to required.

steps.title: The authenticator signs
steps.narration: The **authenticator** verifies the user, then *signs the challenge* with the private **passkey**. It **never shares a secret** with the website — only a signature leaves the device.
steps.say: The authenticator unlocks with the user's biometrics or PIN and signs the challenge with the private key. Critically, it never shares the secret itself with the website.

steps.title: Verify the signature
steps.narration: The browser returns the **signature**; the server verifies *user presence*, *user verification*, and the signature against the **public key**. Passkeys are *unguessable* and **domain-tied**.
steps.say: The browser returns the signature to the server, which verifies user presence, user verification, and the signature against the stored public key. Unguessable, and resistant to phishing.

chapters.title: Layering the Factors
chapters.blurb: Combining independent factors, and a recap of the journey from password to passkey.

story.title: Layering the Factors
story.subtitle: How one user proves who they are, from passwords to passkeys.

steps.title: Layering the Factors
steps.narration: The strongest sign-ins **combine independent factors**. We close by *layering them* and re-tracing the path from password to passkey.
steps.say: Finally, we combine independent factors into one layered sign-in, and re-trace the whole journey.
steps.coverSubtitle: Combine independent factors, and re-trace the whole journey from password to passkey.

steps.title: One user, one sign-in
steps.narration: The user reaches the **app server** to sign in. The method *depends entirely on the application's security requirements*.
steps.say: Our user arrives at the app server one last time. The choice of factors depends entirely on the application's security requirements.

steps.title: Factor one: knowledge
steps.narration: **Factor one** is *knowledge*: the **password**, checked against its salted hash. Alone, it is *likely sufficient* for a casual forum or browser game.
steps.say: The first factor is knowledge, the password the server checks against its salted hash. On its own, it suits a casual forum or browser game.

steps.title: Factor two: possession
steps.narration: **Factor two** is *possession*: a **one-time code** by email, SMS, or authenticator app. Two independent factors give *reasonable security for most users*.
steps.say: When attackers have real incentive, add a second, independent factor: possession, a one-time code by email, S M S, or an authenticator app.

steps.title: Or one strong passkey
steps.narration: For *high security*, a **passkey** can replace the pair: it proves a **physical device plus verification** in one step, and can itself be a *combination of two factors*.
steps.say: For particularly high security, a single passkey can stand in for the pair, proving a physical device plus a PIN or biometrics in one fast step.

steps.title: Access granted
steps.narration: With the factors verified, the server creates an **authenticated session**. The advice: *support both email-based authentication and passkeys*, letting users **choose either**.
steps.say: Once the required factors check out, the server grants an authenticated session. The page recommends supporting both email-based sign-in and passkeys, letting users choose.

steps.title: The whole journey
steps.narration: **Recap:** one user, proven by *knowledge* (`password`), *possession* (`one-time code`), and a *passkey*, each leading to an **authenticated session**. Layer the factors your *risk* demands.
steps.say: So here is the whole path our user travelled: a password proven against a salted hash, a possession factor as a one-time code, and a passkey, any of which lead to one authenticated session. Choose the layers your application's risk demands.
